region: Tropical regions worldwide (Central and South America, Africa, Madagascar, South and Southeast Asia)
description: True rosewoods are the Dalbergia genus, dense and often oily hardwoods used for guitar fretboards and backs, woodwind instruments, furniture, turnery and inlay. Common woodworking species include East Indian rosewood (D. latifolia), Brazilian rosewood (D. nigra), cocobolo (D. retusa) and African blackwood (D. melanoxylon); the trade name 'rosewood' is also applied to many non-Dalbergia woods.

hazards.summary: Patch testing has confirmed allergic skin reactions to rosewood in musicians and instrument makers, with dust-borne rashes in the makers and cross-reactions between different Dalbergia woods. Case reports for East Indian rosewood (D. latifolia) describe hand dermatitis in a wood turner and airborne dermatitis from its dust.
The UK HSE lists rosewoods (many species) as a reported cause of dermatitis, noting that effects can arise just from handling the wood.
The UK HSE also lists rosewoods (many species) as a reported cause of respiratory disorders, without naming a specific mechanism.

Occupational asthma confirmed by inhalation challenge has been reported for Brazilian rosewood (D. nigra), and respiratory allergy for cocobolo (D. retusa). Evidence for other rosewoods is not established.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses after long-term exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.

exposure_limits.note: Applies to wood dust generally; this species has no separate ACGIH value.

known_compounds.name: dalbergiones (e.g. 4-methoxydalbergione)
known_compounds.role: quinone allergens shared across Dalbergia woods, thought to explain cross-reactions

related_species_note: See the separate pages for cocobolo (Dalbergia retusa) and Brazilian rosewood (Dalbergia nigra). Many woods sold as 'rosewood' (e.g. Bolivian rosewood/pau ferro, Machaerium) are not Dalbergia; check the botanical name.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed East Indian rosewood (Dalbergia latifolia) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Heartwood a deep purplish brown to dark chocolate with faint darker purple-black streaks; a stripe of pale yellowish-cream sapwood along one edge. Mostly straight to shallowly interlocked grain with a medium, even texture, small open pores and a subtle natural luster. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of East Indian rosewood with deep purple-brown heartwood and a stripe of pale sapwood.
notes_internal: Genus page. Level 1 skin hazard rests on Pfohler-2018 (positive patch test to an unspecified 'rosewood' recorder) and Gamboa-2024 (sensitisation patterns and cross-reactivity across Dalbergia woods; species list not in abstract). Piletta/Gallo/Athavale (D. latifolia) are title-level only. Level 1 respiratory is species-specific to D. nigra (GodnicCvar-1990); Eaton-1973 testing unconfirmed. Yang 2015 (PMID 25944249) reports occupational toxic epidermal necrolysis linked to D. cochinchinensis; not added, needs full review. HSE 'dermatitis' typed as skin_sensitizer and 'respiratory disorders' as respiratory_irritant; HSE does not say which mechanism.
